tldr: Evaluating the reliability of VLMs as robot task judges on FailBench—a real-world-oriented benchmark spanning 14 data sources—revealed that even the top-performing model achieved only a 77% balanced accuracy, plunging to near-chance levels (<60%) on contact-intensive assembly tasks involving fine physical interactions.
overview:
Because robot learning experiments generate massive numbers of rollouts, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as judges for automated policy evaluation and data filtering is rapidly gaining popularity. However, prior benchmarks have typically evaluated these judges within single, specific datasets, leaving their cross-domain generalization in real-world deployment poorly understood.

To address this, the authors built FailBench, a new benchmark comprising 2,197 manipulation attempts collected across 14 public data sources (12 real-world, 2 simulated). Unlike existing evaluation suites, FailBench moves beyond intentionally curated failures by heavily featuring naturally occurring failures (75% of all failure cases) and high-quality real-world data originally collected for purposes other than failure detection.

Comprehensively testing 13 VLMs (general-purpose models, embodied models, and failure-detection-specialized models) on this dataset showed that the best-performing model, Gemini 3 Flash, attained a macro-averaged balanced accuracy of only 0.77. Even more strikingly, specialized models fine-tuned for failure detection consistently underperformed their own pretrained baselines as well as general-purpose VLMs. While models can identify coarse object movement, their accuracy plummets to below 0.60 (essentially near chance) on fine contact judgments, such as whether fingertips made contact or whether a pin was fully seated.

On the other hand, the authors showed that an input-level preprocessing step—where the VLM itself identifies and crops the outcome-relevant region—improved the top model's score by +2.3 percentage points without extra training, highlighting the critical importance of how visual evidence is presented to the model.
contributions: Constructing FailBench, a cross-domain benchmark assembling 2,197 real-world and simulated manipulation attempts from 14 independent public sources, centered on naturally occurring failures.

Fairly comparing 13 VLMs—from general-purpose to failure-detection-specialized models—under a unified protocol, quantitatively demonstrating that specialized fine-tuning actually harms out-of-domain generalization.

Analyzing the extreme performance gap between recognizing coarse object displacement and judging fine physical contact, and identifying a systematic model bias toward assuming success under ambiguous visual evidence.
Introducing an evidence-localization pipeline that crops outcome-relevant regions, boosting judge accuracy by +2.3 percentage points without any model retraining.

sections.heading: Can We Really Trust VLMs to Judge Robot Success and Failure?
sections.summary: VLM judges are increasingly treated as ground truth for self-improvement and data filtering, yet their cross-domain reliability has remained untested. FailBench, aggregating diverse real-world failures, reveals that even the best model achieves only 0.77 balanced accuracy and struggles severely with contact-rich tasks.
sections.details:
Running robot learning experiments accumulates hundreds or thousands of rollout trials. Because manually checking which trials succeeded is prohibitively expensive for humans, a growing body of research feeds task instructions and execution videos into VLMs, using their verdicts directly for policy evaluation, reward calculation, and training data filtering. However, how reliable these judgments remain once stepping outside the specific dataset where the detector was developed has not been verified at all.

Existing failure detection benchmarks suffer from two major shortcomings. First, they are collected by a single research group within a single robot environment. Second, they rely heavily on synthetic or staged failures—such as abruptly perturbing trajectories midway or intentionally swapping language instructions—which are far detached from real operational failures (e.g., coming up a few millimeters short of insertion, or fingertips failing to make contact and grasping air).

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces FailBench, gathering 2,197 attempts across 14 public sources (12 of which are real-world). Focusing on execution failures and utilizing the original ground-truth labels from each source, the authors benchmarked 13 VLMs across domains. The results uncovered a sobering reality: even the strongest model achieved a balanced accuracy of only 0.77, and models specifically fine-tuned for failure detection consistently fell far short of general-purpose models.

sections.heading: Prior Failure Benchmarks Were Trapped in Single Domains
sections.summary: Previous failure detection research has been confined to single data collection setups and leaned heavily on artificial errors. Meanwhile, policy-dependent monitors inspecting internal states and brute-force human evaluations exist, but scalable, general-purpose evaluation frameworks remained unestablished.
sections.details:
Efforts to use VLMs as robot judges span many areas, including reward design, policy ranking, and retry triggering. Yet many studies integrate these detectors into pipelines without sufficiently scrutinizing the detector's own performance.

Most existing failure benchmarks (such as Guardian, RoboFAC, and ViFailback) were collected under static environments: a single robot, fixed camera viewpoints, and a narrow set of tasks. Furthermore, because many rely on synthetic failures—such as reversing successful videos or substituting text instructions—models risk detecting artifacts of the data generation process rather than true physical task completion. In addition, conflating planning failures (choosing an inappropriate action in the first place) with execution failures (failing while attempting the correct action) has obscured true outcome-judging capability.

On the other hand, policy-dependent monitors track internal representations or action distribution variances, but they are tied to specific model architectures and policies and cannot transfer across platforms. Double-blind human evaluation is the most reliable gold standard, but its steep cost usually limits studies to comparing only 20 to 30 rollouts, making statistical significance hard to achieve. For these reasons, an urgent need arose to evaluate the true capabilities of policy-agnostic VLM judges—which evaluate outcomes purely from camera video and language instructions—across diverse real-world data.

sections.heading: Assembling FailBench: 2,197 Attempts Across 14 Data Sources
sections.summary: FailBench unifies instructions, video, and binary success/failure labels from 14 data sources (12 real, 2 simulated). Overall, 54% of samples are failures, and 75% of those failures occurred naturally during experiments.
sections.details:
To construct FailBench, the authors screened roughly 30 candidate datasets against three criteria: recordings had to capture the trial through to task completion, ground-truth outcome labels had to be provided by the original creators, and tasks or robot types could not overlap redundantly with existing entries. This yielded 14 final data sources.

Because the appearance of a failure varies drastically depending on how it arose, the sources are categorized into three routes:
- **Organic**: Failures that occurred naturally during autonomous rollouts or standard teleoperation on physical hardware (e.g., UR5FAIL, RoboArena, RH20T, REASSEMBLE).
- **Planned**: Failures intentionally induced by a human operator during teleoperation (e.g., BotFails, RoboFAC, REFLECT).
- **Synthetic**: Negative examples synthesized post-hoc by perturbing trajectories of successful rollouts or thresholding quality scores (e.g., BDV2Fail, RoboReward).

Tasks span tabletop pick-and-place, pushing, household chores, contact-intensive assembly on the NIST task board, and cable insertion with low-cost arms. The robots include both single-arm and bimanual setups across various arm models. Camera viewpoints also cover diverse modalities used in practice, including single fixed exterior cameras, multi-view setups featuring wrist cameras, and paired initial/final image frames.

To prevent skew, each source was subsampled to roughly a 50:50 success-to-failure ratio, fixing the total benchmark at 2,197 samples (1,176 failures, 1,021 successes). Thorough quality control was enforced by manually inspecting approximately 25% of all samples and replacing any ambiguous labels with alternate samples from the same source.

sections.heading: General VLMs Dominate, Contact Tasks Falter, and Cropping Helps
sections.summary: Across 13 evaluated models, Gemini 3 Flash led with 0.77 accuracy, while specialized models lagged far behind general-purpose ones. Models solved object displacement but were near chance on physical contact; however, cropping to target regions improved accuracy by +2.3 points.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The authors evaluated 13 models: 6 general-purpose VLMs (Gemini 3 Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it, GPT-4o, and three sizes of Qwen3-VL-Thinking), 2 embodied models (Hy-Embodied variants), and 5 failure-detection-specialized models (Guardian, RoboReward-8B, ViFailback-8B, etc.). The primary evaluation metric is Balanced Accuracy (chance level is 0.50), which is unaffected by class balance shifts.

### 4.2 Results
The top score was 0.77 by Gemini 3 Flash (misjudging roughly one out of every four rollouts), followed by Gemma-4-31B-it at 0.76. Remarkably, all five specialized models built specifically for failure detection underperformed every general-purpose model, with only the smallest general-purpose baseline as an exception. Some specialized models exhibited extreme bias, predicting failure almost regardless of input.
Task characteristics also caused dramatic performance disparities. On the precision assembly dataset "reassemble" using the NIST task board, the mean score across all models sank to 0.52, and even the top-performing model reached only 0.60.
Comparing simulation and real-world subsets, model rankings correlated very strongly (Spearman's $\rho=0.95$), but simulation scores were on average 1.3 points higher with smaller variance between models. This indicates that selecting a detector on a simulator does not guarantee it will perform equally well on real hardware.

### 4.3 Inter-Model Agreement
Measuring whether different models failed on the same samples via the IoU of their error sets (intersection over union) revealed an average IoU of only 0.28 across all model pairs. This low agreement shows models rely on distinctly different visual cues and knowledge. However, combining the top three models in a majority-vote ensemble reached only 0.78 (+0.01 over the best single model), failing to justify the 3x inference cost.

### 4.4 Performance Boost via Evidence Localization
One reason VLMs fail to read subtle physical states from pixels is that the critical region deciding success (such as fingertips or contact points) often occupies only dozens of pixels in the overall image. To address this, the authors tested a localization pipeline: the VLM first predicts a bounding box around the task-relevant critical region, and the fixed-camera video is cropped to that rectangle before being fed to the judge. Testing this with Gemini 3 Flash improved its macro-averaged balanced accuracy from 0.773 to 0.797 (+2.3 percentage points, McNemar's test $p=0.0015$) without retraining. This intervention proved particularly effective on subsets with wide fields of view and small target objects.

sections.heading: Scope of the Study and Remaining Limitations
sections.summary: This benchmark is restricted to binary execution outcome judgments decipherable from video, leaving out planning errors and progress tracking. It also focuses solely on visual inputs from tabletop robot arms, leaving force/tactile sensing, humanoids, and multi-fingered hands for future work.
sections.details:
The findings in this study come with several assumptions and boundaries:

- **Scope of Detailed Error Analysis**: Deep qualitative analysis and inspection of reasoning traces focused primarily on Gemma-4-31B-it, where thought traces were openly accessible; whether identical mechanisms occur in all other models remains an extrapolation.
- **Constrained Task Scope**: The benchmark is strictly confined to a single binary label per attempt, judging execution outcome. It does not evaluate the validity of action plans, intermediate progress estimation, or the ability to articulate causes of failure in natural language.
- **Input Modalities**: While some underlying datasets record force/torque signals or contact audio, inputs were restricted exclusively to vision and text instructions to align with standard VLM usage.
- **Robot Morphology Bias**: All evaluated setups feature tabletop manipulators with parallel-jaw grippers, excluding humanoids, mobile manipulators, and multi-fingered dexterous hands.

sections.heading: Toward Next-Generation Judges That Break the Contact Barrier
sections.summary: Future directions include expanding to humanoids and dexterous hands, integrating multimodal signals like force and audio, and evaluating failure cause categorization. Models must also be developed to explicitly reason about fine spatial and contact relations.
sections.details:
Looking ahead, the authors plan to expand FailBench to more complex robot morphologies, such as humanoids and multi-fingered hands. They also aim to leverage failure cause annotations from original datasets to move beyond simple pass/fail outcomes into failure reason classification.

Additionally, integrating non-visual sensory signals such as force/torque and audio represents a promising path to help judges perceive true contact states that remain indistinguishable from vision alone.

From a model design perspective, the proposed region-cropping approach merely filters out irrelevant background; it does not instill an understanding of physical contact. Bridging the gap on contact-heavy assembly tasks will require exploring novel architectures and training objectives that explicitly reason about fine-grained spatial and contact interactions.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Do Not Overtrust VLM Judges Without Cross-Domain Testing
sections.summary: FailBench demonstrates that while VLMs can track object displacement, they struggle severely with physical contact. High accuracy within a development dataset does not imply generalization, making rigorous verification across diverse, independent environments essential.
sections.details:
This paper presented FailBench, a cross-domain benchmark designed to measure the reliability of VLMs in judging robot manipulation outcomes. Across 2,197 attempts spanning 14 data sources, even state-of-the-art VLMs achieved a mean balanced accuracy of just 0.77, proving that automating outcome evaluation remains an open problem.

A key takeaway is that failure-detection-specialized models showed worse generalization than their own pretrained baselines, and while judgments based on coarse object motion are saturating, performance on tasks requiring physical contact detection degrades to near chance. While input-level evidence cropping provided a notable boost (+2.3 points), it does not fundamentally solve contact perception.

Evaluating a judge model solely within its training domain drastically overestimates its true capability. When integrating VLMs into evaluation loops or reward functions, practitioners must exercise extreme caution to verify whether model judgments are grounded in physical reality.

sections.heading: Appendix: Why Specialized Models Failed and What VLMs Miss
sections.summary: Specialized models previously reported inflated scores due to evaluation set class imbalance, dropping to chance level once balanced. Qualitative analysis further revealed that VLMs exhibit strong confirmation bias, frequently confabulating success while overlooking physical errors.
sections.details:
### B.1 Score Validation: Why Do Numbers Diverge from Prior Literature?
Investigating why specialized models scored drastically lower than their originally reported numbers revealed severe class imbalance in prior evaluation sets. For instance, RoboFAC-7B reported an 80.6% accuracy in its original paper, but 79.7% of its original test set consisted of failure samples. When evaluated on FailBench's balanced subset (30 failures, 30 successes), the model correctly identified all 30 failures but classified 28 out of 30 successes as failures (a success recall of only 6.7%). In short, simply predicting failure on every input yielded an apparent ~80% accuracy on the original skewed test set. Once the class ratio is corrected to 50:50, its actual capability is indistinguishable from random guessing.
Furthermore, directly comparing specialized models against their original base models (such as InternVL and Qwen) under identical prompts showed that all five specialized models scored worse than their un-finetuned baselines. Heavy fine-tuning for failure detection appeared to degrade the models' general perceptual and reasoning abilities.

### B.2 Qualitative Error Analysis: Confirmation Bias and Viewpoint Traps
A detailed look into Gemma-4-31B-it's reasoning traces revealed that while the model reliably identified semantic mistakes (e.g., grasping a blue bowl instead of the requested red one), it consistently missed purely physical failures, such as grippers closing on empty air, objects slipping loose mid-motion, or insufficient insertion depth.
Most prominent was a strong confirmation bias under ambiguous visual evidence: the model defaulted to assuming the instructed action had succeeded, going so far as to confabulate non-existent events. Increasing the thinking budget did not resolve this confirmation bias; instead, the model often generated elaborate post-hoc rationalizations to justify erroneous conclusions. The authors also observed severe viewpoint dependence: if the end-effector visually occluded an object in just one camera view of a multi-view setup, the model frequently ruled success, even when two other views clearly showed the object remained untouched on the table.

captions.F2: Figure F2: Example of confabulation on an apple-in-bowl task (REFLECT). Around $t=63$s, the apple slips from the gripper, and the bowl remains completely empty in the final frame; however, Gemma-4-31B-it with a thinking trace misclassified this trial as a success.
captions.F3: Figure F3: Example of viewpoint-dependent failure on a food-boxing task from ur5fail. The gripper never closed and failed to grasp the grape (yellow bounding box). While camera 1 makes the gripper appear over the grape due to occlusion, cameras 2 and 3 clearly show the grape left behind on the table. Despite having access to all views, the model judged the attempt as a success.

takeaways: Evaluating VLM judge accuracy solely on in-domain data is hazardous; practitioners should expect substantial performance drops when generalizing to unseen robots and tasks.

Specialized failure-detection models often suffer from overfitting and severe class-imbalance bias; using raw frontier general-purpose models (like Gemini 3 Flash) off the shelf is generally far more dependable than fine-tuning.

Current VLMs can track coarse object motion but perform near chance (<60% accuracy) on millimeter-level physical contact, making purely visual VLMs ill-suited for rewards or evaluation in precision assembly and grasp verification.
When target objects appear small relative to camera field of view, an evidence-localization preprocessing pipeline that crops key regions can boost accuracy without any model retraining.
limitations: Outcome judging is formulated strictly as a single binary (0 or 1) label over an entire video, omitting evaluations of high-level planning errors, intermediate progress tracking, or detailed failure reason explanations.
Model inputs are restricted to visual streams and language instructions, leaving out force/torque and acoustic signals that provide vital cues for contact verification.
Evaluations are limited to tabletop manipulators equipped with parallel-jaw grippers, leaving generalization across complex setups like humanoids and dexterous hands unverified.
